name: Santa María Quiegolani Zapotec
confidence_why: Regnier 1993, the only phonology of the language, puts stress on the last syllable of polysyllabic words with a single lexical exception, and Black 1995 agrees that word prominence is rightmost (final root in compounds, second syllable of a disyllabic root) while adding a weight condition that draws stress to a heavy initial syllable, so the two accounts differ only on that detail and there are n…
readall_conflicts: Neither listed work could be opened, so the two Black syntax works contribute nothing. Two open supplementary sources held by the project disagree in detail: Regnier 1993 (SIL-UND Work Papers 37, fn. 3 p. 39 and section 5.1 p. 51) says 'In polysyllabic words stress almost always occurs on the last syllable' and 'When two-syllable words occur, the stress is on the second syllable, as in ca4'yet2 basket', with one exception ('nwjider 'acorn woodpecker', initial stress, possibly onomatopoeic or monosyllabic) — this matches the catalog's final-stress rule (final stress). Black 1995 (SIL-UND Work Papers 39, p. 19 = PDF p. The foot is therefore a quantity-sensitive iamb built on the root. In compounds, stress is on the final root, indicating that word prominence is rightmost.' Black's rule is a weight-sensitive iamb on the root (final root in compounds), which is compatible with Regnier's final-stress observation for most disyllables (nearly all of which are compounds or loans) but predicts root-initial stress when the first root syllable is heavy. So the sources differ on type (fixed: final syllable vs weight-sensitive iambic), not on the typical surface position.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, final: final stress, in the dominant set, not in the strict set) rests on the language's only phonology, Regnier 1993, written by the resident field linguist, with an explicit stress section. The PDF was not yet obtained before; I downloaded it from the cited the Internet Archive URL and confirmed the quotation verbatim at p. 39 fn. 3 and p. 51 sec. 5.1. The text supports exactly the catalog's reading: final stress in polysyllables with one lexical exception (possibly monosyllabic/onomatopoeic), most words monosyllabic, most disyllables compounds or Spanish loans. No later or instrumental description of Quiegolani stress was found in Glottolog or on the web; Black's 1994/2000 syntax works are the only larger descriptions and are print-only, so they are low-priority works still to obtain that are unlikely to change the classification. sources.quote: Most QZ words are monosyllabic. In polysyllabic words stress almost always occurs on the last syllable. ... When two-syllable words occur, the stress is on the second syllable, as in ca'Yet 'basket'. The exception to this rule is the word 'nwjider 'acorn woodpecker', where stress falls on the first syllable.
